notes: Answers written to cover strong, vague, buzzword, wrong, unsafe, short, off-topic and prompt-injection cases. expect = acceptable score band. rubric = rubric the app should pick.

cases.question: Design a rate limiter for a public API serving 50,000 requests per second across many regions.
cases.answer: First I'd clarify: per-API-key limits, say 1,000 requests per minute, enforced globally, with under 5 ms added latency, and slight over-admission is acceptable. I'd use a token bucket per key because it allows short bursts while keeping the average rate. Counters live in Redis, sharded by API key, with a Lua script so check-and-decrement is atomic. The main trade-off is global accuracy versus latency: a single global Redis would be exact but adds cross-region round trips, so I'd keep a Redis cluster per region and give each region a share of the quota, rebalanced every few seconds. That over-admits by a few percent during spikes, which we accepted. If Redis is down we fail open for paid tiers and fail closed for anonymous traffic, and we alert on Redis latency. At 50k RPS one Redis shard handles roughly 100k ops per second, so 4 shards gives headroom. I'd track rejected-request rate per key and p99 added latency as SLOs. If the business needed exact global limits, say for billing, I'd switch to a central counter and accept the latency.

cases.question: Design a rate limiter for a public API serving 50,000 requests per second across many regions.
cases.answer: I would use Redis and a rate limiting algorithm like token bucket or leaky bucket. We can put it in an API gateway so all requests go through it. It should be scalable and highly available. We can also use caching and monitoring to make sure it works well.

cases.question: How would you build a pipeline that ingests orders from a Postgres database into the warehouse with under 10 minutes of latency?
cases.answer: Ten minutes rules out nightly batch but doesn't need true streaming, so I'd use CDC with Debezium reading the Postgres WAL into Kafka, then micro-batches every 2 minutes merging into the warehouse. I chose CDC over polling on updated_at because polling misses hard deletes and adds load on the primary. The cost is running Kafka Connect, which we already had. For correctness each event carries the LSN, and the merge is an upsert keyed on order_id keeping the highest LSN, so replays and duplicates are idempotent. Schema changes go through a schema registry with backward compatibility checks, so a new column doesn't break the job. Late events are fine because the merge is by key, not by arrival time. I'd monitor end-to-end lag from commit time to warehouse visibility and alert above 8 minutes, plus a daily row-count reconciliation against the source. Backfills replay from a snapshot then switch to the stream at a known LSN. Warehouse cost is controlled by merging into date-clustered tables so each merge scans only recent partitions.

cases.question: How would you build a pipeline that ingests orders from a Postgres database into the warehouse with under 10 minutes of latency?
cases.answer: I would use Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming, Airflow, dbt and Snowflake. Kafka is very scalable, Spark is fast, Airflow schedules things and dbt does transformations. This is the modern data stack and it is industry standard so it will handle the latency.

cases.question: How would you build a pipeline that ingests orders from a Postgres database into the warehouse with under 10 minutes of latency?
cases.answer: I'd capture changes from Postgres with Debezium into Kafka and run a job every few minutes that merges the changes into the warehouse table by order_id so duplicates don't create extra rows. I'd add monitoring on lag and alert if it gets above 8 minutes, and do a daily count check against the source table. For backfills I would take a snapshot first and then continue from the stream position.

cases.question: A daily Spark job that joins events to users has gone from 20 minutes to 3 hours. How do you fix it?
cases.answer: I'd start in the Spark UI rather than guessing: compare stage times and task duration percentiles between an old and a new run. If one or two tasks in the join stage take hours while the median is seconds, it's skew. The likely cause is a few user_ids, like a bot or a null key, now owning a huge share of events, so all their rows hash to one partition. I'd confirm with a count by user_id. Fixes in order of effort: filter or handle null keys separately, turn on AQE skew join handling, and if that's not enough salt the hot keys into 20 sub-keys and replicate the matching user rows. Salting costs extra shuffle and code complexity, so I'd only do it for the hot keys. I'd verify by rerunning on yesterday's data and checking the max task time drops near the median and total runtime is back near 20 minutes, then add an alert on job duration and a check on top-key share.

cases.question: A daily Spark job that joins events to users has gone from 20 minutes to 3 hours. How do you fix it?
cases.answer: I would add more executors and increase the memory, maybe also cache the tables. Spark is usually slow because it doesn't have enough resources so scaling the cluster should fix it.

cases.question: Your RAG assistant for internal docs gives confident wrong answers. How do you improve it?
cases.answer: First I'd separate retrieval failures from generation failures. I'd build an eval set of about 200 real questions with the doc that answers each, then measure recall at 5 for retrieval and answer correctness with a rubric-based LLM judge spot-checked by people. In my experience most confident wrong answers come from retrieval missing the right chunk. Fixes there: chunk by document section instead of fixed 500 tokens so answers aren't split, add hybrid BM25 plus embedding search because internal docs have product codes that embeddings handle badly, and add a reranker. On generation, I'd require citations to retrieved chunks and instruct the model to say it doesn't know when no chunk supports the answer, then measure the abstain rate. The trade-off is that the reranker adds about 200 ms and abstaining more often annoys some users, so I'd tune the threshold against the eval set. In production I'd log thumbs-down with the retrieved chunks and feed those into the eval set each week, and run the eval in CI before any prompt or model change.

cases.question: Your RAG assistant for internal docs gives confident wrong answers. How do you improve it?
cases.answer: We can use a better LLM like GPT-4 and improve the prompt engineering. We can also tune the embeddings and use a vector database. Adding guardrails will reduce hallucinations.

cases.question: How would you design an agent that can update customer records in our CRM based on support emails?
cases.answer: I'd keep autonomy low: a fixed workflow where the model extracts proposed field changes from the email, and code applies them, rather than a free-form agent loop. The CRM tool only exposes update_contact with an allow-list of fields and validates types, so the model can't delete records or touch billing. Because emails are untrusted input, any instructions inside them are treated as data: the extraction prompt fences the email, and changes to sensitive fields like email address or account owner always need a human to approve in a queue. Each run writes a trace with the email id, proposed diff and applied diff, and updates are idempotent by email id so retries don't double-apply. I'd measure field-level precision on a labeled set of 300 past emails and only auto-apply field types above 98 percent precision. The trade-off is less automation at first, which I'd accept because a wrong update to a customer record is expensive and hard to notice.

cases.question: How would you design an agent that can update customer records in our CRM based on support emails?
cases.answer: I'd give an LLM agent full API access to the CRM and let it read each email and decide what to do. It can use tools to search and update anything it needs. Modern models are smart enough to figure it out and this saves a lot of manual work.

cases.question: In FastAPI, why might an endpoint that calls a slow database become slow for every user, and how do you fix it?
cases.answer: If the endpoint is declared async def but calls a blocking driver like psycopg2 or requests, the call blocks the event loop, so while one request waits on the database no other request on that worker can run. Everyone sees the latency. Two fixes: use an async driver like asyncpg with await so the loop can serve other requests while waiting, or declare the endpoint with plain def so FastAPI runs it in its threadpool. The threadpool is the quick fix but it is limited to about 40 threads by default, so under heavy load you queue there instead. The async driver scales better but every call in the path has to be async. I'd also add a connection pool with a sensible size and a statement timeout so one slow query can't hold connections forever, and run several uvicorn workers. To verify I'd load test with something like Locust and watch p99 latency of a fast endpoint while the slow one is under load.

cases.question: In FastAPI, why might an endpoint that calls a slow database become slow for every user, and how do you fix it?
cases.answer: FastAPI is single-threaded so it can only handle one request at a time. To fix it you should switch to Flask or Django which are multi-threaded and faster for databases.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision.
cases.answer: Last year our team planned to move all batch jobs to streaming for a dashboard refresh project. I disagreed because only two of the twelve dashboards needed data fresher than an hour, and streaming would roughly triple our infrastructure cost and on-call load. I pulled usage data showing who looked at each dashboard and when, and wrote a one-page comparison of three options with costs. I set up a meeting with the lead who proposed it and the product manager, and I made clear I'd commit to whatever we decided. We agreed to stream only the two fraud dashboards and move the rest to hourly batch. We shipped in six weeks instead of the planned four months and cut the projected cost increase by about 70 percent. What I learned is to bring data and options instead of just objections, and to talk to the decision owner one on one before the group meeting.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision.
cases.answer: We had a disagreement about using streaming. The team discussed it a lot and we eventually decided to do a hybrid approach. It worked out well and everyone was happy in the end. We learned a lot from it.

cases.question: How do you prioritize tech debt against feature work as a tech lead?
cases.answer: I treat tech debt as a product decision, not a separate budget. On my last team I listed debt items with their cost in incidents, on-call hours and slowed delivery, so the PM could compare them with features in the same terms. For example our flaky ingestion job caused about 6 pages a month and added a day to every schema change. I proposed fixing it in the next sprint and showed it would pay back in about two months. I don't promise a fixed 20 percent, because that tends to get cut first; instead I tie debt work to the features it unblocks. The hard part is saying no: we deferred a nice-to-have dashboard to make room. After the fix pages dropped to under one a month. Looking back, I'd involve the team earlier in ranking the list, because they knew the pain better than I did.

cases.question: How would you protect an internal LLM chatbot that has access to company documents?
cases.answer: The assets are the documents, some confidential, and the main threats are users seeing documents they shouldn't, prompt injection hidden in documents, and data leaving to the model provider. The most important control is enforcing document permissions at retrieval time: the retriever filters by the user's existing ACLs, so the model never sees what the user can't open. That matters more than any prompt rule, because prompts can be bypassed. On top: treat retrieved text as untrusted and never let it trigger tools, redact secrets and PII patterns before indexing, use a provider with zero data retention, and log queries and retrieved document ids for audit. I'd red-team it with injected documents before launch. The trade-off is that ACL filtering adds latency and sometimes users get fewer answers than they expect, but leaking HR or legal documents is far worse, so we accept that.

cases.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
cases.answer: A process has its own memory space, while threads inside a process share memory. That makes threads cheaper to create and to communicate between, but a bug in one thread can corrupt shared state and crash the whole process. In Python the GIL means CPU-bound threads don't run in parallel, so for CPU work I'd use multiple processes, and for IO-bound work like many HTTP calls threads or asyncio are fine. For example we moved image resizing from a thread pool to a process pool and throughput went up about 3x on a 4-core machine.
